questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Ramon, 50 years old, operated a hardware store and was killed in a vehicular accident through a bus driver's negligence. His heirs proved by his income tax documents that his gross annual income was ₱600,000; there is no evidence of his business expenses or living expenses. Following Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee, compute the indemnity for his loss of earning capacity.

suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee, the Court held that indemnity for loss of earning capacity under Article 2206 is awarded not for loss of earnings but for loss of capacity to earn money, and that only net earnings are considered: the earnings less expenses necessary to produce them, less living and other incidental expenses. Absent documentary evidence of expenses, it pegged necessary business expenses at 80% of the gross income and living expenses at 50% of the net income, using: Net Earning Capacity = 2/3 (80 − age at death) × (Gross Annual Income − necessary expenses), less living expenses.
suggestedAnswer.application: Life expectancy: 2/3 × (80 − 50) = 2/3 × 30 = 20 years. Gross annual income ₱600,000, less 80% necessary expenses (₱480,000) = ₱120,000. Less living expenses of 50% (₱60,000) = ₱60,000. Net earning capacity: 20 × ₱60,000 = ₱1,200,000.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The heirs are entitled to ₱1,200,000. **Bar trap:** for a business owner, deduct first the expenses necessary to earn the income, then living expenses; never multiply the gross income by the life expectancy. (Compare People v. Muyco, where 80% of the gross income of a farm laborer was deducted as living expenses.)

keyPoints: Art. 2206 indemnity is for loss of capacity to earn, not loss of earnings
Only net earnings: gross income less necessary expenses, less living expenses
Absent evidence: necessary expenses at 80% of gross; living expenses at 50% of net

source.caseTitle: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
source.part: Decision, computation of loss of earning capacity (net earnings)
source.excerpt: The indemnity for loss of earning capacity of the deceased is provided for by Article 2206 of the Civil Code. Compensation of this nature is awarded not for loss of earnings, but for loss of capacity to earn money. … In the computation of loss of earning capacity, only net earnings, not gross earnings, are to be considered; that is, the total of the earnings less expenses necessary for the creation of such earnings or income, less living and other incidental expenses. In the absence of documentary evidence, it is reasonable to peg necessary expenses for the lease and operation of the gasoline station at 80 percent of the gross income, and peg living expenses at 50 percent of the net income (gross income less necessary expenses). In this case, the computation for loss of earning capacity is as follows: Net Earning Capacity = Life Expectancy [2/3 (80-age at the time of death)] x Gross Annual Income (GAI) – Reasonable and Necessary Expenses (80% of GAI) X = [2/3 (80-65)] x ₱1,000,000.00 - ₱800,000.00 X = 2/3 (15) x ₱200,000.00 - ₱100,000.00(Living Expenses) X = 30/3 x ₱100,000.00 X = 10 x ₱100,000.00 X = ₱1,000,000.00

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A bus driver saw a motorcycle ahead on the left side of the highway but kept his speed and veered left, hitting the motorcycle and a parked jeep. Sued with the driver, the bus company proves that the driver passed NBI clearance, a certification from his previous employer, a physical examination, a driving test and reviews of his driving skill every six months. The driver admitted prior sideswiping incidents, which the company did not know about. (a) Was the driver negligent? (b) Is the company liable?

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Yes; the driver failed to take the precaution an ordinary reasonable person would have taken against a foreseeable risk. (b) Yes; the company did not overcome the presumption that it failed to exercise the diligence of a good father of a family in the selection and supervision of its driver.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee, the Court held that foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence: a defendant is negligent if he acted or failed to act in such a way that an ordinary reasonable man would have realized that certain interests of certain persons were unreasonably subjected to a general but definite class of risks. Whenever an employee's negligence causes damage, there instantly arises a presumption that the employer failed to exercise due diligence in the selection or supervision of its employees; to avoid liability the employer must present convincing proof of that diligence.
suggestedAnswer.application: (a) Having seen the motorcycle ahead, the driver should have slowed down; instead he kept his speed and veered into the left lane. (b) The company's tests focused only on driving ability and physical fitness; it did not sufficiently inculcate discipline and correct road behavior, and did not even know of the driver's sideswiping history. That is not convincing proof of diligence in supervision.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The driver was negligent and the company is solidarily liable. **Bar trap:** passing hiring tests (selection) does not prove diligent supervision; the employer must show both.

keyPoints: Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence
The driver saw the motorcycle but did not slow down and veered left
An employee's negligence raises a presumption of the employer's negligence in selection or supervision
The employer must overcome it by convincing proof
Tests limited to driving ability and fitness, and ignorance of prior incidents, do not suffice

source.caseTitle: Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee
source.part: Decision, negligence of the driver and liability of the employer
source.excerpt: Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence. To be negligent, a defendant must have acted or failed to act in such a way that an ordinary reasonable man would have realized that certain interests of certain persons were unreasonably subjected to a general but definite class of risks. In this case, the bus driver, who was driving on the right side of the road, already saw the motorcycle on the left side of the road before the collision. However, he did not take the necessary precaution to slow down, but drove on and bumped the motorcycle, and also the passenger jeep parked on the left side of the road, showing that the bus was negligent in veering to the left lane, causing it to hit the motorcycle and the passenger jeep. Whenever an employee’s negligence causes damage or injury to another, there instantly arises a presumption that the employer failed to exercise the due diligence of a good father of the family in the selection or supervision of its employees. To avoid liability for a quasi-delict committed by his employee, an employer must overcome the presumption by presenting convincing proof that he exercised the care and diligence of a good father of a family in the selection and supervision of his employee. The Court upholds the finding of the trial court and the Court of Appeals that petitioner is liable to respondent, since it failed to exercise the diligence of a good father of the family in the selection and supervision of its bus driver, Margarito Avila, for having failed to sufficiently inculcate in him discipline and correct behavior on the road. Indeed, petitioner’s tests were concentrated on the ability to drive and physical fitness to do so. It also did not know that Avila had been previously involved in sideswiping incidents.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Only the defendant bus company appealed a judgment awarding the plaintiff loss of earning capacity, funeral expenses and moral damages for her husband's death. The Court of Appeals added civil indemnity for the death, temperate damages for her damaged motorcycle (whose repair cost was shown only by a job estimate), and moral damages for her own physical injuries, all of which she had prayed for in her complaint. The company argues that the plaintiff did not appeal. Was the Court of Appeals correct? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. An appellate court may review matters not assigned as errors if their consideration is necessary for a just decision, and each added award had a legal basis.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee, the Court applied Section 8, Rule 51 of the Rules of Civil Procedure: errors not assigned may be considered if they affect jurisdiction or the validity of the judgment, are closely related to or dependent on an assigned error, or are plain or clerical errors; and the appellate court is clothed with ample authority to review matters not assigned if necessary to arrive at a just decision. Civil indemnity for death is proper under Article 2206; temperate damages may be recovered under Article 2224 when some pecuniary loss is shown but its amount cannot be proved with certainty; and moral damages may be recovered in quasi-delicts causing physical injuries under Article 2219.
suggestedAnswer.application: The trial court overlooked damages the plaintiff had prayed for. The damage to the motorcycle was certainly caused by the driver's negligence, but a job estimate is not competent proof of its actual cost, so ₱10,000 temperate damages was reasonable. The plaintiff's own injuries supported moral damages (reduced by the Supreme Court to ₱30,000 per prevailing jurisprudence), and the death supported ₱50,000 civil indemnity.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The Court of Appeals was correct. **Bar trap:** the general rule that only assigned errors are reviewed has exceptions; and a job estimate supports temperate, not actual, damages.

keyPoints: Sec. 8, Rule 51: unassigned errors may be considered in certain cases
The appellate court may review matters not assigned if necessary for a just decision
Civil indemnity for death (Art. 2206)
Temperate damages when loss is certain but its amount unproven (Art. 2224); a job estimate is not proof of actual cost
Moral damages for physical injuries in quasi-delicts (Art. 2219)

source.excerpt: In addition, the Court of Appeals correctly awarded temperate damages in the amount of ₱10,000.00 for the damage caused on respondent’s motorcycle. Under Art. 2224 of the Civil Code, temperate damages "may be recovered when the court finds that some pecuniary loss has been suffered but its amount cannot, from the nature of the case, be proved with certainty." The cost of the repair of the motorcycle was prayed for by respondent in her Complaint. However, the evidence presented was merely a job estimate of the cost of the motorcycle’s repair amounting to ₱17, 829.00. … The Court of Appeals also correctly awarded respondent moral damages for the physical injuries she sustained due to the vehicular accident. Under Art. 2219 of the Civil Code, moral damages may be recovered in quasi-delicts causing physical injuries. … Further, the Court of Appeals correctly awarded respondent civil indemnity for the death of her husband, which has been fixed by current jurisprudence at ₱50,000.00. The appellate court is clothed with ample authority to review matters, even if they are not assigned as errors in the appeal, if it finds that their consideration is necessary in arriving at a just decision of the case.

choices.A: the actual earnings the deceased received before his death.
choices.B: the mental anguish of the heirs.
choices.C: the loss of capacity to earn money, not the loss of earnings.
choices.D: the funeral and burial expenses.

choices.A: Foreseeability.
choices.B: Last clear chance.
choices.C: Res ipsa loquitur.
choices.D: Proximate cause.

questions.explanation: **A is correct.** The Court said: "Foreseeability is the fundamental test of negligence. choices.B: Gross earnings less taxes only.
choices.C: The earnings claimed in the complaint.

It pegged necessary expenses at 80% of gross and living expenses at 50% of net, absent documentary evidence. **A, B and C are wrong** for the same reason. **Bar trap:** income claimed without documentary proof (like the copra business in this case) is not counted.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: As explained in Philippine Hawk Corporation v. Lee, what is the purpose of moral damages?

choices.A: To punish the defendant for the public good.
choices.B: To enrich the plaintiff at the expense of the defendant.
choices.C: To allow the plaintiff to obtain means, diversions or amusements that will alleviate the moral suffering caused by the defendant's culpable action; they must be proportional to the suffering inflicted.
choices.D: To replace the plaintiff's lost income.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said: "Moral damages are not intended to enrich a plaintiff at the expense of the defendant. They are awarded to allow the plaintiff to obtain means, diversions or amusements that will serve to alleviate the moral suffering he/she has undergone due to the defendant's culpable action and must, perforce, be proportional to the suffering inflicted." **A is wrong:** that describes exemplary damages. **B is wrong:** the Court expressly said they are not meant to enrich. **D is wrong:** lost income is covered by actual damages or loss of earning capacity. **Bar trap:** moral damages compensate, not punish.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A 35-year-old employee earning ₱20,000 a month, as shown by his payslips, was murdered. The trial court awarded actual, moral and exemplary damages and civil indemnity, but nothing for loss of earning capacity, since the heirs did not appeal. Following People v. Asilan, may the appellate court award it, and how much?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Under Article 2206, the defendant is liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, which in every case shall be assessed and awarded by the court. Computed as in Asilan: ₱3,600,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In People v. Asilan, the Court held that both lower courts failed to consider that under Article 2206 the accused is also liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, payable to his heirs, and awarded it on appeal. It used: Net Earning Capacity = life expectancy × (gross annual income − living expenses) = 2/3 (80 − age at death) × (gross annual income − 50% of gross annual income), net income being gross income less living expenses.
suggestedAnswer.application: Life expectancy: 2/3 × (80 − 35) = 2/3 × 45 = 30 years. Gross annual income: ₱20,000 × 12 = ₱240,000. Less 50% living expenses (₱120,000) = ₱120,000. Net earning capacity: 30 × ₱120,000 = ₱3,600,000. The payslips satisfy the requirement of documentary proof.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The appellate court should award ₱3,600,000 for loss of earning capacity. **Bar trap:** the award is mandatory under Article 2206 when proven, even if the trial court overlooked it; and the living-expense deduction used in Asilan (50% of gross) differs from that used in Muyco (80% of gross), so follow the facts and the approach of the decision cited.

keyPoints: Art. 2206: liability for loss of earning capacity, assessed and awarded by the court in every case
The appellate court may award it even if the lower courts failed to
Formula used in Asilan: 2/3 (80 − age) × (gross annual income − 50% living expenses)
Documentary proof of income (payslips) supports the award

The loss of earning capacity of Asilan is thus computed as follows: Net Earning Capacity = life expectancy x [gross annual income – living expenses] = 2/3 [80-age at time of death] x [gross annual income – 50% of gross annual income] = 2/3 [80-29] x [₱ 103,260.00 – ₱ 51,630.00] = 34 x ₱ 51,630.00 = ₱ 1,755,420.00

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: What are the factors in computing the damages recoverable for the loss of earning capacity of a deceased person? When may such indemnity NOT be awarded under Article 2206 of the Civil Code? Explain, following People v. Asilan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The factors are: (1) the number of years on the basis of which the damages shall be computed, using the formula 2/3 × (80 − age of the deceased at death) = life expectancy, adopted from the American Expectancy Table of Mortality; and (2) the rate at which the losses sustained by the heirs should be fixed, that is, the net income (gross income less living expenses). The indemnity is not awarded when the deceased, on account of permanent physical disability not caused by the defendant, had no earning capacity at the time of his death.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: People v. Asilan quoted Article 2206: the amount of damages for death caused by a crime or quasi-delict shall be at least three thousand pesos, even if there are mitigating circumstances; in addition, (1) the defendant shall be liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, paid to the heirs, and such indemnity shall in every case be assessed and awarded by the court, unless the deceased on account of permanent physical disability not caused by the defendant had no earning capacity at the time of his death. The Court then listed the two factors.
suggestedAnswer.application: So in every death caused by a crime or quasi-delict, the court must determine the deceased's life expectancy and net income, unless he had no earning capacity because of a permanent disability not caused by the defendant (for example, if he was already permanently incapacitated from an earlier, unrelated cause).
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Two factors: life expectancy and net income; the only exception is lack of earning capacity due to a permanent disability not caused by the defendant. **Bar trap:** a disability caused by the defendant himself does not excuse him from this indemnity.

keyPoints: Factor 1: number of years, life expectancy = 2/3 × (80 − age at death), from the American Expectancy Table of Mortality
Factor 2: the rate of loss, net income = gross income less living expenses
Art. 2206: indemnity shall in every case be assessed and awarded by the court
Exception: the deceased had no earning capacity because of a permanent physical disability not caused by the defendant

source.caseTitle: People v. Asilan
source.part: Discussion, loss of earning capacity (the factors and Article 2206)
source.excerpt: Art. 2206. The amount of damages for death caused by a crime or quasi-delict shall be at least three thousand pesos, even though there may have been mitigating circumstances. In addition: (1) The defendant shall be liable for the loss of the earning capacity of the deceased, and the indemnity shall be paid to the heirs of the latter; such indemnity shall in every case be assessed and awarded by the court, unless the deceased on account of permanent physical disability not caused by the defendant, had no earning capacity at the time of his death; … The following are the factors in computing the amount of damages recoverable for the loss of earning capacity of the deceased: 1) The number of years on the basis of which the damages shall be computed. This is based on the formula (2/3 x 80 – age of the deceased at the time of his death = life expectancy), which is adopted from the American Expectancy Table of Mortality; and 2) The rate at which the losses sustained by the heirs of the deceased should be fixed. Net income is arrived at by deducting the amount of the victim’s living expenses from the amount of his gross income.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In a murder qualified by treachery, the trial court ordered the accused to pay the victim's heirs ₱84,224 actual damages based on receipts and a list, ₱25,000 moral damages and ₱50,000 civil indemnity. How did the Court modify the damages in People v. Asilan, and on what bases?

suggestedAnswer.answer: Civil indemnity was increased to ₱75,000 and moral damages to ₱50,000 per prevailing jurisprudence; ₱30,000 exemplary damages were added because of treachery; actual damages were fixed at ₱80,224, the total of the receipts; ₱1,755,420 was added for loss of earning capacity; and 6% interest per annum was imposed on all damages from finality.

Asilan, the Court increased civil indemnity and moral damages "[p]ursuant to prevailing jurisprudence"; awarded exemplary damages "in view of the presence of the qualifying circumstance of treachery" under Article 2230 of the Civil Code; fixed actual damages on the widow's receipts for hospital and funeral expenses; and applied Article 2206 for loss of earning capacity.
suggestedAnswer.application: The receipts showed ₱25,224 hospital, ₱35,000 memorial and ₱20,000 funeral expenses, totaling ₱80,224. The victim, 29, earned ₱8,605 a month (₱103,260 a year), shown by documentary evidence; with 50% living expenses deducted and 34 years of life expectancy, the loss was ₱1,755,420.

Exemplary damages of ₱30,000 under Art. 2230 because of treachery

Loss of earning capacity of ₱1,755,420 under Art. 2206
6% interest on all damages from finality

questions.prompt: The accused in People v. Asilan returned to the scene of the stabbing instead of fleeing. How did the Court treat this?

choices.A: As proof of his innocence.
choices.B: As not implying innocence: flight is indicative of guilt, but its converse is not necessarily true, since some culprits stay nearby to create a semblance of regularity.
choices.C: As a mitigating circumstance of voluntary surrender.
choices.D: As grounds to doubt the eyewitnesses.

questions.explanation: **B is correct.** The Court said his "failure to flee and the apparent normalcy of his behavior subsequent to the commission of the crime do not imply his innocence," because "[f]light is indicative of guilt, but its converse is not necessarily true. Culprits behave differently … while others may remain in the same vicinity so as to create a semblance of regularity." **A and D are wrong** for the same reason. **C is wrong:** he was arrested after being pointed out by a witness; no voluntary surrender was found. **Bar trap:** non-flight is not proof of innocence.

source.caseTitle: People v. Asilan
source.part: Discussion, credibility of the evidence (flight)
source.excerpt: In the same manner, it is also not surprising that Asilan returned to the scene of the crime after stabbing Adovas. His "failure to flee and the apparent normalcy of his behavior subsequent to the commission of the crime do not imply his innocence." This Court, elucidating on this point, declared: Flight is indicative of guilt, but its converse is not necessarily true. Culprits behave differently and even erratically in externalizing and manifesting their guilt. Some may escape or flee -- a circumstance strongly illustrative of guilt -- while others may remain in the same vicinity so as to create a semblance of regularity, thereby avoiding suspicion from other members of the community.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: The accused in People v. Asilan argued for the first time on appeal that he could only be convicted of homicide because the Information did not specify how treachery was carried out. How did the Court rule?

choices.A: It reduced the crime to homicide.
choices.B: It remanded the case for amendment of the Information.
choices.C: It rejected the argument: treachery was specifically alleged, and in any case his failure to move to quash before pleading waived objections to the Information's sufficiency, the deficiency having been cured by evidence presented without objection.
choices.D: It held that qualifying circumstances need not be alleged at all.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court found that "the qualifying circumstance of 'treachery' was specifically alleged in the Information," and that under Section 9, Rule 117, the failure to move to quash before pleading is a waiver of objections (save specified grounds); citing People v. Candaza, an Information lacking essential allegations may still sustain a conviction when the accused fails to object during trial and the deficiency is cured by competent evidence. **A and B are wrong** for those reasons. **D is wrong:** the Court reiterated that qualifying circumstances must be properly pleaded. **Bar trap:** object to a defective Information before pleading, or the objection is generally waived.

source.excerpt: Contrary to Asilan’s contention, the qualifying circumstance of "treachery" was specifically alleged in the Information. "The rule is that qualifying circumstances must be properly pleaded in the Information in order not to violate the accused’s constitutional right to be properly informed of the nature and cause of the accusation against him." … Moreover, in People v. Candaza, this Court held that "[a]n Information which lacks essential allegations may still sustain a conviction when the accused fails to object to its sufficiency during the trial, and the deficiency was cured by competent evidence presented therein."

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish attorney's fees awarded as an item of damages under Article 2208 of the Civil Code from the attorney's fees that a lawyer claims from his own client for professional services, as explained in Quirante v. Intermediate Appellate Court.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Attorney's fees under Article 2208 are an item of damages awarded in favor of the litigant, not of his counsel; the litigant is the judgment creditor who may enforce them by execution against the losing party. Attorney's fees for professional services, on the other hand, arise from the contract between the lawyer and the client, with the lawyer as creditor and the client as debtor.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Quirante v. IAC, the Court held that what the petitioners claimed as attorney's fees was "different from attorney's fees as an item of damages provided for under Article 2208 of the Civil Code, wherein the award is made in favor of the litigant, not of his counsel, and the litigant, not his counsel, is the judgment creditor who may enforce the judgment for attorney's fees by execution." The petitioners' claims were based on an alleged contract for professional services.
suggestedAnswer.application: Thus the ₱30,000 attorney's fees awarded against the contractor and its surety in the main judgment belonged to the client as damages, while Atty. Quirante's claim for a share of the recovery under his agreement with the client was a separate claim against the client and his heirs.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Article 2208 fees go to the client and are paid by the losing party; professional fees go to the lawyer and are paid by the client. **Bar trap:** a lawyer cannot treat the Article 2208 award as automatically his own; it is the client's damages.

keyPoints: Art. 2208 attorney's fees: an item of damages awarded to the litigant, who is the judgment creditor
Paid by the losing party; enforceable by the litigant through execution
Fees for professional services: based on the lawyer-client contract
There the lawyer is the creditor and the client the debtor

Here, the petitioner's claims are based on an alleged contract for professional services, with them as the creditors and the private respondents as the debtors.

May he claim his fees in the same action? Should the court confirm them now? Explain.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: After the client died, his widow and two of his daughters signed a document confirming a fee agreement between him and his lawyer; the other heirs did not sign. The appellate court ruled that the confirmation could not adversely affect the heirs who did not sign. How did the Supreme Court treat this ruling in Quirante v. Intermediate Appellate Court?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Supreme Court rejected that portion of the appellate court's ruling as premature and pre-emptive; the effect of the confirmation on all the heirs should be determined by the trial court after the entire case is adjudicated.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Quirante v. IAC, the Court held that the orderly administration of justice dictates that the effect of the alleged confirmation by some heirs be determined by the trial court, as it involves the same contingencies in determining the propriety and extent of the fees. The trial court will be in a better position, after adjudicating the entire case (including the surety's liability and the heirs' respective participations in the award), to determine with evidentiary support matters such as whether the agreement with the deceased binds all his heirs.
suggestedAnswer.application: Ruling now that the non-signatory heirs are not bound would pre-empt factual and evidentiary matters that should first be presented to the trial court, and it rests on the same premise (an eventual award) that made the confirmation premature.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The question was left for the trial court after final adjudication, and the appellate court's holding on non-signatories was rejected. **Bar trap:** the Supreme Court affirmed the result (setting aside the confirmation) but not every reason the appellate court gave.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In a collection suit between two banks, the trial court discussed only the claim for lost opportunity and the interest in the body of its decision, then stated in the dispositive portion: "defendant is ordered to pay plaintiff attorney's fees of ₱10,000." No other explanation was given. On appeal, the defendant bank questions the award. Should the award be sustained? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The award of attorney's fees should be deleted because the court did not state its factual, legal and equitable justification in the text of its decision.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Philippine National Bank v. Court of Appeals, the Court held that the discretion to award attorney's fees under Article 2208 of the Civil Code "demands factual, legal and equitable justification, without which the award is a conclusion without a premise and improperly left to speculation and conjecture." The reason for the award must be stated in the text of the decision; if it is stated only in the dispositive portion, it shall be disallowed. Since the award is an exception rather than the rule, the court must make findings of fact and law that bring the case within the exception.
suggestedAnswer.application: The trial court gave no reason in the body of its decision for the ₱10,000 award; it appeared only in the dispositive portion. Without findings bringing the case under one of the exceptions in Article 2208, the award has no premise.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The award must be deleted, even though the rest of the judgment stands. **Bar trap:** winning the case does not by itself entitle the winner to attorney's fees; the award is the exception and must be justified in the body of the decision.

keyPoints: Attorney's fees under Art. 2208: within the court's discretion, but it demands factual, legal and equitable justification
The reason must be stated in the text of the decision

source.caseTitle: Philippine National Bank v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the award of attorney's fees
source.excerpt: However, the amount of P10,000.00 as attorney's fees is hereby deleted. In their respective decisions, the trial court and the Court of Appeals failed to explicitly state the rationale for the said award. … The award of attorney's fees lies within the discretion of the court and depends upon the circumstances of each case. However, the discretion of the court to award attorney's fees under Article 2208 of the Civil Code of the Philippines demands factual, legal and equitable justification, without which the award is a conclusion without a premise and improperly left to speculation and conjecture. It becomes a violation of the proscription against the imposition of a penalty on the right to litigate (Universal Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Intermediate Appellate Court, 188 SCRA 170 [1990]). The reason for the award must be stated in the text of the court's decision. If it is stated only in the dispositive portion of the decision, the same shall be disallowed. questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A drawee bank cleared a government check, then weeks later returned it and refused to pay, because the check's serial number had been altered. The name of the issuing agency was printed on the face of the check, and the drawer, payee and amount were unchanged. Is the change of the serial number a material alteration that justifies the dishonor? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The alteration of the serial number is not a material alteration, so the drawee bank had no right to dishonor the check.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Philippine National Bank v. Court of Appeals, the Court held that an alteration is material if it alters the effect of the instrument; a material alteration is one which changes the items required to be stated under Section 1 of the Negotiable Instruments Law. The serial number is not an essential requisite of negotiability under Section 1.
suggestedAnswer.application: The change did not alter the relations between the parties: the drawer and drawee were unchanged, the payee was the same and the sum due was the same. The issuing agency was sufficiently identified because its name was printed on the check, so the serial number was redundant for that purpose.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The alteration was innocent, the check remained negotiable in all respects, and the drawee bank could not dishonor and return it. **Bar trap:** not every unauthorized change is material; test it against the requisites in Section 1 of the Negotiable Instruments Law.

keyPoints: Material alteration: one that alters the effect of the instrument
It changes the items required to be stated under Section 1 of the NIL
A check's serial number is not an essential requisite of negotiability
Parties, payee and amount were unchanged; the issuer was printed on the check
No material alteration, so no right to dishonor

source.caseTitle: Philippine National Bank v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the first issue (material alteration)
source.excerpt: An alteration is said to be material if it alters the effect of the instrument. It means an unauthorized change in an instrument that purports to modify in any respect the obligation of a party or an unauthorized addition of words or numbers or other change to an incomplete instrument relating to the obligation of a party. In other words, a material alteration is one which changes the items which are required to be stated under Section 1 of the Negotiable Instruments Law. … The case at bench is unique in the sense that what was altered is the serial number of the check in question, an item which, it can readily be observed, is not an essential requisite for negotiability under Section 1 of the Negotiable Instruments Law. The aforementioned alteration did not change the relations between the parties. The name of the drawer and the drawee were not altered. The intended payee was the same. The sum of money due to the payee remained the same.

Court of Appeals, the Court agreed with the Court of Appeals that the certification deserved no weight: the person who signed it was not presented to prove that he prepared it and that the signature was his, and no eyewitness to its execution was presented to identify it.
suggestedAnswer.application: Without the testimony of the signatory or a witness to its execution, the court cannot rule on the authenticity of the contents of the certification. In any case, the alleged alteration (the serial number) was not material.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The certification was properly disregarded. **Bar trap:** a document signed by a public officer is not automatically proof of its contents when its due execution has not been established.

No eyewitness to its execution identified it
Without this proof, the authenticity of its contents cannot be ruled upon
Besides, the serial number change was not a material alteration

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: B borrowed ₱500,000 from L under a promissory note that was silent on interest. On maturity, L sent B a written demand, which B ignored. L sued, and the court ordered B to pay the ₱500,000. Applying the rules laid down in Eastern Shipping Lines v. Court of Appeals: (a) Is B liable for interest even though the note did not stipulate it? From when? (b) What happens once the judgment becomes final and executory but B still does not pay?

suggestedAnswer.answer: (a) Yes. Although no conventional interest is due without a written stipulation, B owes legal interest as damages for his delay, computed from default, that is, from L's extrajudicial demand. (b) From the finality of the judgment until it is satisfied, legal interest runs on the amount due, because that period is treated as equivalent to a forbearance of credit.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Eastern Shipping Lines v. CA (rule II.1): when an obligation consisting of a loan or forbearance of money is breached, the interest due is that stipulated in writing; in the absence of stipulation, the rate (12% in 1994) is computed from default, i.e., from judicial or extrajudicial demand, under Article 1169. Rule II.3: when a judgment awarding a sum of money becomes final and executory, the legal rate applies from such finality until satisfaction, this interim period being deemed equivalent to a forbearance of credit.
suggestedAnswer.application: The obligation is a loan. With no written stipulation, legal interest applies as damages, and it runs from L's written demand, which put B in default. After the judgment becomes final, interest continues on the amount due until B pays.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Interest runs from the extrajudicial demand, and from finality until full payment. **Bar trap:** the absence of a written stipulation bars only conventional (stipulated) interest, not legal interest as damages for delay. Also, the 12% rate stated in this 1994 case was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013 (BSP Circular No. 799, applied in Nacar v. Gallery Frames); always check the current rate.

keyPoints: Loan or forbearance: the interest stipulated in writing applies
No stipulation: legal interest as damages, from default (judicial or extrajudicial demand, Art. 1169)
Interest due itself earns legal interest from judicial demand
From finality of the judgment until satisfaction: legal interest, as the period is equivalent to a forbearance of credit
The 12% rate was later lowered to 6% (from July 1, 2013); check the current rate

source.caseTitle: Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, the rules of thumb on interest (rule II.1 and II.3)
source.excerpt: 1. When the obligation is breached, and it consists in the payment of a sum of money, i.e., a loan or forbearance of money, the interest due should be that which may have been stipulated in writing. Furthermore, the interest due shall itself earn legal interest from the time it is judicially demanded. In the absence of stipulation, the rate of interest shall be 12% per annum to be computed from default, i.e., from judicial or extrajudicial demand under and subject to the provisions of Article 1169 of the Civil Code. … 3. When the judgment of the court awarding a sum of money becomes final and executory, the rate of legal interest, whether the case falls under paragraph 1 or paragraph 2, above, shall be 12% per annum from such finality until its satisfaction, this interim period being deemed to be by then an equivalent to a forbearance of credit.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A consignee's goods were damaged in transit. Its insurer demanded payment of the loss from the carrier, then sued. The amount of the loss was disputed and was fixed only by the trial court after trial. The insurer asks for legal interest from the filing of the complaint. Applying Eastern Shipping Lines v. Court of Appeals, from when should interest run, and on what amount? Explain.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Interest should run from the date of the trial court's judgment, not from the filing of the complaint, and it should be computed on the amount finally adjudged.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Eastern Shipping Lines v. CA (rule II.2): when an obligation not constituting a loan or forbearance of money is breached, interest on the damages may be imposed at the court's discretion (6% a year). No interest is adjudged on unliquidated claims or damages except when or until the demand can be established with reasonable certainty. Where it is so established, interest runs from judicial or extrajudicial demand; where it cannot be reasonably established at the time of demand, interest runs only from the date of the judgment, when the damages may be deemed reasonably ascertained. The base is in any case the amount finally adjudged.
suggestedAnswer.application: The claim is for damage to goods, not a loan or forbearance. Since the amount was disputed and became reasonably certain only when the trial court fixed it, interest runs from that judgment. That is how the Court modified the award in Eastern Shipping itself: 6% from the trial court's decision, then 12% from finality.

source.excerpt: 2. When an obligation, not constituting a loan or forbearance of money, is breached, an interest on the amount of damages awarded may be imposed at the discretion of the court at the rate of 6% per annum. questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Goods shipped in good order arrived damaged after passing through the custody of the carrier, the arrastre operator and the customs broker, in that order. Sued with the others, the carrier argues that it cannot be held liable because no court made an express finding that it was negligent, and the damage might have occurred while the goods were with the others. Is the carrier's argument correct? Explain, citing Eastern Shipping Lines v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The carrier is presumed at fault, and no express finding of negligence is needed to hold it liable.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Eastern Shipping Lines v. CA, the Court held that the carrier's duty of diligence lasts from the time the goods are unconditionally placed in its possession until delivered to the person entitled to receive them (Arts. 1736-1738, Civil Code). When the goods are lost or arrive damaged, a presumption arises against the carrier of its failure to observe that diligence, and there need not be an express finding of negligence (Art. 1735). The exceptions in Article 1734 are exclusive. Both the arrastre operator and the carrier are charged with the obligation to deliver the goods in good condition to the consignee.
suggestedAnswer.application: The damage happened while the goods were in the successive custody of the carrier and the others, and the carrier did not rebut the presumption of fault or show any Article 1734 cause. Its liability is inevitable regardless of whether others are solidarily liable with it.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The carrier is liable. **Bar trap:** the Court did not say that the arrastre operator and broker are always solidarily liable with the carrier; that depends on the facts. What is fixed is the presumption against the carrier.

keyPoints: The carrier's duty lasts from receipt until delivery to the person entitled to receive the goods
Goods lost or damaged: presumption of the carrier's fault; no express finding of negligence needed (Art. 1735)
The exceptions in Art. 1734 are exclusive
Carrier and arrastre operator are both bound to deliver the goods in good condition
Solidary liability of arrastre and broker is not automatic; facts may vary the rule

source.caseTitle: Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the carrier's liability
source.excerpt: The common carrier's duty to observe the requisite diligence in the shipment of goods lasts from the time the articles are surrendered to or unconditionally placed in the possession of, and received by, the carrier for transportation until delivered to, or until the lapse of a reasonable time for their acceptance by, the person entitled to receive them (Arts. 1736-1738, Civil Code; Ganzon vs. Court of Appeals, 161 SCRA 646; Kui Bai vs. Dollar Steamship Lines, 52 Phil. 863). When the goods shipped either are lost or arrive in damaged condition, a presumption arises against the carrier of its failure to observe that diligence, and there need not be an express finding of negligence to hold it liable (Art. 1735, Civil Code; Philippine National Railways vs. Court of Appeals, 139 SCRA 87; Metro Port Service vs. Court of Appeals, 131 SCRA 365). There are, of course, exceptional cases when such presumption of fault is not observed but these cases, enumerated in Article 1734 of the Civil Code, are exclusive, not one of which can be applied to this case. … We do not, of course, imply by the above pronouncement that the arrastre operator and the customs broker are themselves always and necessarily liable solidarily with the carrier, or vice-versa, nor that attendant facts in a given case may not vary the rule. The instant petition has been brought solely by Eastern Shipping Lines, which, being the carrier and not having been able to rebut the presumption of fault, is, in any event, to be held liable in this particular case.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: S agreed to sell a lot to B in a conditional sale. B paid ₱2 million in advance, but S never fulfilled the conditions she undertook. The contract provided only that the down payment would be returned if S failed, and said nothing about interest. After B's written demand, S still kept the money. B sues for the ₱2 million plus 12% interest. S argues that (1) no interest is due since none was stipulated, and (2) at most 6% applies because the contract is a sale, not a loan. Rule on S's arguments, citing Estores v. Spouses Supangan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Both arguments fail. Interest may be imposed without a stipulation, and the rate is that for a forbearance of money (12% when Estores was decided), running from B's demand until full payment.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Estores v. Spouses Supangan, the Court held that under Article 2210, interest may in the court's discretion be allowed upon damages awarded for breach of contract, and the seller was in default from the date of demand. On the rate, the phrase "forbearance of money, goods or credits" has a meaning separate from a loan: it refers to arrangements other than loans where a person acquiesces to the temporary use of his money pending the happening of certain events or the fulfillment of conditions. The buyers parted with their money before the conditions were fulfilled, and the seller's unwarranted withholding of it amounts to a forbearance of money, an involuntary loan, so the rate applicable to a loan applies.
suggestedAnswer.application: B parted with the ₱2 million before S fulfilled the conditions, allowing her the use of it. When the conditions failed and S kept the money despite demand, B was deprived of its use. B is entitled to the return of the principal and to compensation for its use, at the forbearance rate, from the demand.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Interest is due at the forbearance rate from demand. **Bar trap:** a contract that is not a loan can still involve a forbearance of money; do not stop at the name of the contract. Note also that the 12% rate applied in Estores was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013 (BSP Circular No. 799, Nacar v. Gallery Frames); check the current rate.

keyPoints: Interest may be awarded on damages for breach of contract without stipulation (Art. 2210)
Default from the date of demand
Forbearance has a meaning separate from a loan
Forbearance: acquiescing to the temporary use of one's money pending events or conditions
Unwarranted withholding of the money = forbearance, an involuntary loan; the loan rate applies
The 12% rate was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013

source.caseTitle: Estores v. Spouses Supangan
source.part: Our Ruling, interest at 12% (forbearance of money)
source.excerpt: We sustain the ruling of both the RTC and the CA that it is proper to impose interest notwithstanding the absence of stipulation in the contract. Article 2210 of the Civil Code expressly provides that "[i]nterest may, in the discretion of the court, be allowed upon damages awarded for breach of contract." … We believe however, that the phrase "forbearance of money, goods or credits" is meant to have a separate meaning from a loan, otherwise there would have been no need to add that phrase as a loan is already sufficiently defined in the Civil Code. Forbearance of money, goods or credits should therefore refer to arrangements other than loan agreements, where a person acquiesces to the temporary use of his money, goods or credits pending happening of certain events or fulfillment of certain conditions. In this case, the respondent-spouses parted with their money even before the conditions were fulfilled. They have therefore allowed or granted forbearance to the seller (petitioner) to use their money pending fulfillment of the conditions. They were deprived of the use of their money for the period pending fulfillment of the conditions and when those conditions were breached, they are entitled not only to the return of the principal amount paid, but also to compensation for the use of their money. And the compensation for the use of their money, absent any stipulation, should be the same rate of legal interest applicable to a loan since the use or deprivation of funds is similar to a loan. Petitioner’s unwarranted withholding of the money which rightfully pertains to respondent-spouses amounts to forbearance of money which can be considered as an involuntary loan. Thus, the applicable rate of interest is 12% per annum.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court distinguished Eastern Shipping and Reformina: both were torts cases with no forbearance of money, and the damages claimed could not be established with reasonable certainty when the claim was made. In Estores, there was a forbearance, and the amount (₱3.5 million) and the date of demand were certain, so interest at the forbearance rate ran from the demand until full satisfaction.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Estores v. Spouses Supangan: "Eastern Shipping Lines, Inc. v. Court of Appeals and its predecessor case, Reformina v. Tongol both involved torts cases and hence, there was no forbearance of money, goods, or credits. Further, the amount claimed (i.e., damages) could not be established with reasonable certainty at the time the claim was made." Since the date of demand, September 27, 2000, was satisfactorily established during trial, the 12% rate was reckoned from that date until the principal and interest are fully satisfied.
suggestedAnswer.application: The seller's counsel treats every non-loan obligation as falling under the 6% rule. But the obligation to return a definite sum withheld after demand is a forbearance, and the amount was known from the start, so there is no reason to wait for the judgment.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Interest at the forbearance rate from the date of demand. **Bar trap:** interest runs from the judgment only for claims that were not reasonably certain at demand, as in torts; a fixed sum withheld after demand earns interest from the demand.

In those cases, the damages were not reasonably certain when claimed
Here the amount was fixed and the date of demand established at trial
Interest ran from the demand (September 27, 2000) until full satisfaction

questions.prompt: A buyer forced to sue to recover the advance payment that a defaulting seller refused to return asks for attorney's fees of ₱50,000 plus 20% of whatever is recovered. The seller argues that no attorney's fees are due because the buyer did not win everything it asked for. Are attorney's fees warranted? In what amount? Explain, citing Estores v. Spouses Supangan.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes, attorney's fees are warranted because the buyer was compelled to litigate to protect its interest, but the award must be reasonable; in Estores the Court fixed it at ₱50,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: Under Article 2208 of the Civil Code, attorney's fees may be recovered (2) when the defendant's act or omission has compelled the plaintiff to litigate or to incur expenses to protect his interest, and (11) in any other case where the court deems it just and equitable; in all cases, they must be reasonable. In Estores, the spouses were forced to litigate to recover their money, so they were entitled to attorney's fees, but the Court found ₱50,000 more appropriate, in line with the policy that the award must always be reasonable. The trial court's ₱50,000 plus 20% of the recoverable amount had been found excessive and reduced to ₱100,000 by the Court of Appeals, then further reduced.
suggestedAnswer.application: The seller's refusal to return the money despite demand compelled the buyer to sue. That the buyer did not obtain every amount it asked for does not remove the ground under Article 2208. But the 20% add-on would be excessive.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Attorney's fees of a reasonable amount (₱50,000 in Estores). **Bar trap:** the fact that a party was compelled to litigate justifies the award, but never an unreasonable amount; the court may reduce it.

Art. 2208(11): when just and equitable
In all cases, attorney's fees must be reasonable

However, we find the amount of ₱50,000.00 more appropriate in line with the policy enunciated in Article 2208 of the Civil Code that the award of attorney’s fees must always be reasonable.

questions.prompt: A final judgment ordered the defendants to render an accounting and inventory of a partnership's assets and to deliver to the plaintiff his one-half share. In execution, the plaintiff added 12% interest on his share of the assets from the time the business closed, arguing that his claim was liquidated because it could be determined by mathematical computation. The court of appeals agreed. Is the plaintiff's claim correct? Explain, citing Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The share in the partnership assets was an unliquidated claim that earns no interest until reasonably determined, and it became liquidated only when the trial court approved the accounting.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Sunga-Chan v. CA, the Court agreed that the partner's share and interest in the assets "partake of an unliquidated claim which, until reasonably determined, shall not earn interest for him." The legal norm for interest to accrue is "reasonably determinable," not determinable by mathematical computation, as the Court of Appeals had declared. The judgment's own directive to render an accounting, inventory and appraisal recognized that the exact share could not be determined with reasonable precision without that process; a liquidated claim cannot validly be asserted without accounting.
suggestedAnswer.application: The plaintiff's share could be fixed only after the inventory and accounting. It became liquidated only upon the trial court's approval of the accounting report, after the computation was submitted, so no interest could be added to it.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: No interest on the share of the assets. **Bar trap:** "capable of mathematical computation" is not the test; the test is whether the amount is reasonably determinable, and an amount that needs an accounting is not.

The norm is "reasonably determinable", not "determinable by mathematical computation"
The judgment's order to account shows the share could not be fixed without accounting
A liquidated claim cannot be asserted without accounting
The share became liquidated only when the accounting was approved

source.part: The Court's Ruling, first issue (interest on the share of the partnership assets)
source.excerpt: Anent the impasse over the partnership assets, we are inclined to agree with petitioners’ assertion that Chua’s share and interest on such assets partake of an unliquidated claim which, until reasonably determined, shall not earn interest for him. As may be noted, the legal norm for interest to accrue is "reasonably determinable," not, as Chua suggested and the CA declared, determinable by mathematical computation. The Court has certainly not lost sight of the fact that the October 7, 1997 RTC decision clearly directed petitioners to render an accounting, inventory, and appraisal of the partnership assets and then to wind up the partnership affairs by restituting and delivering to Chua his one-half share of the accounted partnership assets. The directive itself is a recognition that the exact share and interest of Chua over the partnership cannot be determined with reasonable precision without going through with the inventory and accounting process. In fine, a liquidated claim cannot validly be asserted without accounting. In net effect, Chua’s interest and share over the partnership asset, exclusive of the goodwill, assumed the nature of a liquidated claim only after the trial court, through its November 6, 2002 resolution, approved the assets inventory and accounting report on such assets.

questions.prompt: A trial court's judgment, rendered on March 1, 2010, ordered the defendants to pay the plaintiff his unreceived profits from a partnership business, a fixed amount per month, "with legal rate of interest until fully paid." The judgment became final on March 1, 2012, but the defendants did not pay. Following the approach in Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals, what interest should the profits earn, and for which periods?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The profits should earn 6% a year from the date of the trial court's decision (March 1, 2010) until it became final (March 1, 2012); after that, the total profits with the added interest should earn the forbearance rate (12% in Sunga-Chan) from finality until fully paid.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Sunga-Chan v. CA, applying the Eastern Shipping rules, the Court held that the award of earned but unremitted profits "must earn interest at 6% per annum reckoned from October 7, 1997, the rendition date of the RTC decision, until December 20, 2001, when the said decision became final and executory. Thereafter, the total of the monthly profits inclusive of the add on 6% interest shall earn 12% per annum reckoned from December 20, 2001 until fully paid, as the award for that item is considered to be, by then, equivalent to a forbearance of credit."
suggestedAnswer.application: The profits award does not arise from a loan or forbearance, so the 6% rate under Article 2209 applies until finality. Once the judgment is final and unpaid, the period is treated as a forbearance of credit, and the base for the higher rate includes the 6% interest already earned.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: 6% from the decision to finality; then the forbearance rate on profits plus interest until paid. **Bar trap:** after finality, the higher rate applies to the total, including the 6% interest already accrued. Note that the 12% rate was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013 (BSP Circular No. 799, Nacar v. Gallery Frames), so the rate for the period after finality must be checked against the current rule.

keyPoints: Profits award: not a loan or forbearance, so 6% (Art. 2209)
6% from the trial court's decision until finality
From finality: 12% on the profits plus the 6% interest added
After finality the award is equivalent to a forbearance of credit
The 12% rate was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013

source.part: The Court's Ruling, first issue (interest on the unreceived profits)
source.excerpt: Guided by the foregoing rules, the award to Chua of the amount representing earned but unremitted profits, i.e.. PhP 35,000 monthly, from January 1988 until May 30, 1992, must earn interest at 6% per annum reckoned from October 7, 1997, the rendition date of the RTC decision, until December 20, 2001, when the said decision became final and executory. Thereafter, the total of the monthly profits inclusive of the add on 6% interest shall earn 12% per annum reckoned from December 20, 2001 until fully paid, as the award for that item is considered to be, by then, equivalent to a forbearance of credit. Likewise, the PhP 250,000 award, representing the goodwill value of the business, the award of PhP 50,000 for moral and exemplary damages, PhP 25,000 attorney’s fee, and PhP 25,000 litigation fee shall earn 12% per annum from December 20, 2001 until fully paid.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: After their father's death, a widow and her daughter continued a partnership business against the surviving partner's will and refused to account. Held liable to him, they argue that their liability is only joint, so the sheriff could not levy on the daughter's absolute community property with her husband for the whole judgment. Are they correct? Explain, citing Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Their obligation is solidary, and the daughter's absolute community property may answer for it.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Sunga-Chan v. CA, the Court held the obligation solidary because (1) continuing the business against the partner's will gave rise to a solidary obligation, the acts not being severable, a case where the nature of the obligation requires solidarity under Article 1207; (2) the duty to remit his share proceeds from the indivisible obligation to account; and (3) the obligation to pay damages and fees is solidary, the petitioners having resisted in bad faith a legitimate claim. The community property is not exempt from execution, and under Article 94 of the Family Code the absolute community is liable for debts contracted by either spouse without the other's consent to the extent the family benefited; the daughter's use of the business assets may reasonably be considered to have been for her and her husband's benefit.
suggestedAnswer.application: It is impossible to draw the line where one petitioner's liability ends and the other's begins, or to quantify how much each misappropriated. The levy on the daughter's community property for the whole obligation was valid.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Solidary liability; the community property answers. **Bar trap:** solidarity is not presumed (Art. 1207), but it exists when the law or the nature of the obligation requires it, as here.

keyPoints: Solidarity only when the obligation states it, or the law or nature of the obligation requires it (Art. 1207)
The acts complained of were not severable; the duty to account was indivisible
Bad-faith resistance to a legitimate claim: damages and fees solidary
Community property not exempt from execution
Art. 94, Family Code: the community answers to the extent the family benefited

source.caseTitle: Sunga-Chan, et al. v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: The Court's Ruling, second and third issues (solidary liability, community property)
source.excerpt: For one, the complaint of Chua for winding up of partnership affairs, accounting, appraisal, and recovery of shares and damages is clearly a suit to enforce a solidary or joint and several obligation on the part of petitioners. As it were, the continuance of the business and management of Shellite by petitioners against the will of Chua gave rise to a solidary obligation, the acts complained of not being severable in nature. Indeed, it is well-nigh impossible to draw the line between when the liability of one petitioner ends and the liability of the other starts. In this kind of situation, the law itself imposes solidary obligation. … For the other, the duty of petitioners to remit to Chua his half interest and share of the total partnership assets proceeds from petitioners’ indivisible obligation to render an accounting and inventory of such assets. The need for the imposition of a solidary liability becomes all the more pronounced considering the impossibility of quantifying how much of the partnership assets or profits was misappropriated by each petitioner. And for a third, petitioners’ obligation for the payment of damages and attorney’s and litigation fees ought to be solidary in nature, they having resisted in bad faith a legitimate claim and thus compelled Chua to litigate. … Absent any indication otherwise, the use and appropriation by petitioner Sunga-Chan of the assets of Shellite even after the business was discontinued on May 30, 1992 may reasonably be considered to have been used for her and her husband’s benefit.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Under Sunga-Chan v. Court of Appeals, what is the legal norm for interest to accrue on a claim?

choices.A: The claim must be determinable by mathematical computation.
choices.B: The claim must be stated in the complaint.
choices.C: The claim must be reasonably determinable.
choices.D: The claim must be supported by an official receipt.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said: "the legal norm for interest to accrue is 'reasonably determinable,' not, as Chua suggested and the CA declared, determinable by mathematical computation." **A is wrong:** that is the test the Court rejected. **B and D are wrong:** neither is the norm. **Bar trap:** almost anything can be computed once figures are known; the question is whether the amount was reasonably determinable at the time.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A passenger sent an airline an extrajudicial demand on August 1, 2003 for damages for breach of contract of carriage. The trial court, in its judgment of April 25, 2007, awarded him actual damages, ₱1 million moral damages, exemplary damages and attorney's fees. The Court of Appeals imposed 6% legal interest from the date of the extrajudicial demand. The airline argues that interest should run only from the trial court's judgment. Is the airline correct? Explain, citing Air France v. De Camilis.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. The 6% legal interest runs from April 25, 2007, the date of the trial court's judgment, not from the extrajudicial demand; from the finality of the decision, the higher rate applies until full satisfaction.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Air France v. De Camilis, the Court applied Eastern Shipping Lines: for an obligation not constituting a loan or forbearance, no interest is adjudged on unliquidated claims or damages except when or until the demand can be established with reasonable certainty; when such certainty cannot be established at the time of demand, interest runs only from the date of the judgment. The Court held that the interest "shall be reckoned from April 25, 2007 when the RTC rendered its judgment, not from the time of respondent's extrajudicial demand. This must be so as it was at the time the RTC rendered its judgment that the quantification of damages may be deemed to have been reasonably ascertained."
suggestedAnswer.application: The passenger's claims for moral and exemplary damages and attorney's fees could not be fixed with reasonable certainty when he made his demand; their amounts were set only when the trial court decided. So interest runs from that judgment, on all sums awarded.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The airline is correct on the starting date. **Bar trap:** the date of the extrajudicial demand applies only when the amount was already reasonably certain then; damages left to the court's discretion become certain only on judgment. Note too that the 12% rate after finality was later lowered to 6% from July 1, 2013; check the current rate.

keyPoints: Breach of contract of carriage: not a loan or forbearance, so 6%
No interest on unliquidated damages until they can be established with reasonable certainty
Here the damages were reasonably ascertained only when the trial court rendered judgment
Interest runs from the trial court's judgment, not from the extrajudicial demand
From finality, the higher rate until full satisfaction, on all sums awarded

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, discussion of the legal interest
source.excerpt: Pursuant to this ruling, the legal interest is 6% p.a. and it shall be reckoned from April 25, 2007 when the RTC rendered its judgment, not from the time of respondent’s extrajudicial demand. This must be so as it was at the time the RTC rendered its judgment that the quantification of damages may be deemed to have been reasonably ascertained. Then, from the time this decision becomes final and executory, the interest rate shall be 12% p.a. until full satisfaction.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A passenger was refused entry at a transit stop because he did not have the required transit visa. He sues the airline, claiming that its agents should have told him about the visa. The evidence also shows that, afterwards, the airline's agents rudely refused his requests, falsely reported him as a security threat, refused to honor his confirmed flights and treated him with verbal abuse. Is the airline liable? Explain, citing Air France v. De Camilis.

suggestedAnswer.answer: The airline is not liable for the refused entry, because the passenger is responsible for having the correct travel documents; but it is liable for damages for the bad-faith treatment by its agents.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Air France v. De Camilis, the Court of Appeals ruled that it was the passenger, and not the airline, who was responsible for having the correct travel documents, but that this did not absolve the airline from liability for damages. It found that the airline's agents "repeatedly subjected respondent to very poor service, verbal abuse and abject lack of respect and consideration," so the airline was guilty of bad faith. It therefore charged the passenger with his expenses for the Moscow leg, but held the airline liable for his expenses from the false security-threat report to the dishonored Paris-Manila reservation, and affirmed moral damages and attorney's fees. The Supreme Court denied the airline's petition.
suggestedAnswer.application: The missing visa is the passenger's own fault, so his losses from being refused entry are his. But the later abuse by the airline's agents is the airline's breach, committed in bad faith, and supports actual damages for the expenses it caused, as well as moral and exemplary damages.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Liable, but only for the consequences of its agents' bad faith. **Bar trap:** the passenger's fault on one point does not excuse the carrier's separate bad-faith acts; separate the losses by cause.

keyPoints: The passenger is responsible for having the correct travel documents
That did not absolve the airline from liability for damages
Very poor service, verbal abuse and lack of respect by its agents = bad faith
Actual damages limited to expenses caused by the airline's acts; the Moscow leg borne by the passenger
Moral damages and attorney's fees affirmed

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, statement of the Court of Appeals' ruling on liability
source.excerpt: The CA ruled that it was respondent (as passenger), and not AF, who was responsible for having the correct travel documents. However, the appellate court stated that this fact did not absolve AF from liability for damages. The CA agreed with the findings of fact of the RTC that AF’s agents and representatives repeatedly subjected respondent to very poor service, verbal abuse and abject lack of respect and consideration. As such, AF was guilty of bad faith for which respondent ought to be compensated. The appellate court affirmed the award of ₱1 million moral damages and ₱300,000 attorney’s fees. However, it reduced the actual damages to US$906 (or its peso equivalent). According to the CA, this amount represented the expenses respondent incurred from the time he was unable to join his group in Rome (due to the unfounded "communiqué" of Ms. Soeyesol that he was a security threat) up to the time his flight reservation from Paris to Manila was dishonored for which he was forced to stay in Paris for two additional days. The appellate court pointed out that, on the other hand, respondent’s expenses for the Moscow leg of the trip must be borne by him as AF could not be faulted when he was refused entry to Moscow for lack of a transit visa.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Losing on appeal, an airline files a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45, arguing that the passenger's injury was not clearly established and that the moral and exemplary damages and attorney's fees awarded are exorbitant. Will the Supreme Court review the awards? Explain, citing Air France v. De Camilis.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Whether the passenger is entitled to the damages and attorney's fees requires a review of the evidence, which is a question of fact outside a Rule 45 petition, absent any of the recognized exceptions.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Air France v. De Camilis, the Court held that the issue of entitlement to damages and attorney's fees "entails a resort to the parties' respective evidence," so the airline was asking the Court to consider a question of fact. The jurisdiction of the Court in a Rule 45 petition is limited to questions of law, save for certain exceptions, none of which was present. Both the trial court and the Court of Appeals had properly laid down the factual and legal bases for their decisions.
suggestedAnswer.application: The airline's attack on whether the injury was proved, and on the amounts, depends on weighing the evidence. Since the lower courts stated the factual and legal bases of the awards and no exception applies, the Court would not disturb them.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The petition fails on this point; only the interest was clarified. **Bar trap:** a Rule 45 petition cannot be used to re-weigh the evidence on damages; the lower courts' stated bases also distinguish this from an unexplained award of attorney's fees.

keyPoints: Entitlement to damages and attorney's fees requires a resort to the evidence: a question of fact
Rule 45 is limited to questions of law, save for certain exceptions
No exception was present
The lower courts laid down the factual and legal bases for their awards

source.caseTitle: Air France Philippines/KLM Air France v. De Camilis
source.part: Resolution, discussion of the entitlement to damages
source.excerpt: Preliminarily, on the issue pertaining to whether or not respondent was entitled to damages and attorney’s fees, the same entails a resort to the parties’ respective evidence. Thus, AF is clearly asking us to consider a question of fact. Time and again, we have held that the jurisdiction of this Court in a petition for review on certiorari under Rule 45 is limited only to questions of law, save for certain exceptions, none of which are present in this case. Both the RTC and the CA have competently ruled on the issue of respondent’s entitlement to damages and attorney’s fees as they properly laid down both the factual and legal bases for their respective decisions. We see no reason to disturb their findings.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Distinguish attorney's fees in their ordinary concept from attorney's fees in their extraordinary concept. In a suit where the plaintiff wins, may the court award her attorney's fees of ₱107,000 plus ₱1,000 per appearance and ₱10,000 litigation expenses simply because she prevailed? Explain, citing Padillo v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: In the ordinary concept, attorney's fees are the reasonable compensation a client pays his lawyer for legal services. In the extraordinary concept, they are awarded by the court as indemnity for damages, paid by the losing party to the prevailing party. They are not awarded every time a party wins, and an excessive award will be reduced.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Padillo v. CA, the Court held that the award of attorney's fees is the exception rather than the general rule; counsel's fees are not awarded every time a party prevails, because no premium should be placed on the right to litigate. Attorney's fees as part of damages are awarded only in the instances in Article 2208; the court must make findings of fact and law that bring the case within the exception, and in all cases the fees must be reasonable. They are not meant to enrich the winning party at the expense of the losing litigant.
suggestedAnswer.application: Winning the case is not enough. Even where the court finds it just and equitable to award attorney's fees, the amount must be reasonable. In Padillo, the Court found ₱107,000 plus ₱1,000 per appearance and ₱10,000 litigation expenses unreasonable and excessive, and reduced it to ₱25,000.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Not simply because she prevailed; and the amount awarded must be reasonable. **Bar trap:** the extraordinary concept goes to the litigant as damages and is the exception; the ordinary concept is between lawyer and client.

keyPoints: Ordinary concept: reasonable compensation paid by the client to the lawyer
Extraordinary concept: indemnity for damages paid by the losing party to the prevailing party
The exception, not the rule; not awarded every time a party prevails
Only in the cases in Art. 2208, with findings of fact and law; always reasonable
Not meant to enrich the winning party; reduced to ₱25,000 in Padillo
