source.excerpt: With respect to attorney's fees, the award thereof is the exception rather than the general rule; counsel's fees are not awarded every time a party prevails in a suit because of the policy that no premium should be placed on the right to litigate. Attorney's fees as part of damages are not the same as attorney's fees in the concept of the amount paid to a lawyer. In the ordinary sense, attorney's fees represent the reasonable compensation paid to a lawyer by his client for the legal services he has rendered to the latter, while in its extraordinary concept, they may be awarded by the court as indemnity for damages to be paid by the losing party to the prevailing party. Attorney's fees as part of damages is awarded only in the instances specified in Article 2208 of the Civil Code. As such, it is necessary for the court to make findings of facts and law that would bring the case within the exception and justify the grant of such award, and in all cases it must be reasonable. … Attorney's fees as part of damages is not meant to enrich the winning party at the expense of the losing litigant. Thus, it should be reasonably reduced to Twenty-Five Thousand Pesos (P25,000.00).

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: An owner kept out of her commercial lot and building for ten years testified that she could have earned ₱150,000 a year from it, and that the occupant had made millions from it, but gave no details on how such income could be earned. The occupant admitted that he had been paying the former owner a monthly rental of ₱800. How much should the owner recover as actual damages for the lost income? Explain, citing Padillo v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: She should recover only the unrealized rentals at the admitted rate of ₱800 a month for the period of occupancy, not the claimed ₱150,000 a year.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Padillo v. CA, the Court held the claimed ₱150,000 yearly income "highly conjectural and speculative," since the owner did not detail how such income could be derived from the property. Actual, compensatory and consequential damages must be proved and cannot be presumed; if the proof is flimsy and insufficient, no damages will be allowed. The only unrealized income she was entitled to was the monthly rental the occupant admitted, ₱800 a month, for the period he occupied the property.
suggestedAnswer.application: Her bare testimony is too vague and unspecified to support ₱150,000 a year. But the occupant's own admission of the ₱800 monthly rental is competent proof of the loss. In Padillo, that came to ₱97,600 for January 1982 to February 1992, with legal interest from the finality of the decision.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: Only the admitted rentals, with legal interest from finality. **Bar trap:** actual damages are never presumed; a claimant's estimate without supporting details fails, but an admitted figure can still support a smaller award.

keyPoints: Actual damages must be proved and cannot be presumed
Vague, unspecified testimony on expected income is conjectural and speculative
Flimsy or insufficient proof: no damages allowed
The admitted rental (₱800 a month) is the measure of the lost income
₱97,600 for the period of occupancy, with legal interest from finality

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the unrealized income
source.excerpt: Concerning the alleged forgone income of One Hundred Fifty Thousand Pesos (P150,000.00) per year since 1982 as testified on by petitioner as the income she could have realized had possession of the property not been withheld from her by respondent Averia, we consider such amount of expected profit highly conjectural and speculative. With an allegation that respondent made millions for the improper use and exploitation of the property, petitioner's testimony regarding the matter of unrealized income is sadly lacking of the requisite details on how such huge amount of income could be made possible. Petitioner did not detail out how such huge amount of income could have been derived from the use of the disputed lot and building. Well-entrenched is the doctrine that actual, compensatory and consequential damages must be proved, and cannot be presumed. If the proof adduced thereon is flimsy and insufficient, as in this case, no damages will be allowed. Verily, the testimonial evidence on alleged unrealized income earlier referred to is not enough to warrant the award of damages. It is too vague and unspecified to induce faith and reliance. The only amount of unrealized income petitioner should be entitled to is the unrealized monthly rentals which respondent Averia admits to be in the amount of Eight Hundred Pesos (P800.00) a month

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: In an earlier certiorari case between the same parties, the Court of Appeals, instead of dismissing the plaintiff's damages suit for litis pendentia, ordered it merely suspended until a related registration case was finished. No appeal was taken, and that ruling became final. After the plaintiff won the damages suit, the Court of Appeals reversed it on the ground of res judicata, since the requisites were present. Was the reversal correct? Distinguish the law of the case from res judicata, citing Padillo v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Although all the requisites of res judicata were present, the final ruling ordering only the suspension of the damages suit had become the law of the case between the parties, even if erroneous, so the plaintiff could not be faulted for continuing with it.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Padillo v. CA, the Court explained that the law of the case means that whatever is once irrevocably established as the controlling legal rule or decision between the same parties in the same case continues to be the law of the case, whether correct or not, so long as the facts remain the same. It differs from res judicata: the law of the case does not have the finality of res judicata and applies only to that one case, whereas res judicata forecloses parties or privies in one case by what has been done in another case. Since no appeal was taken from the decision ordering suspension instead of dismissal, it became final and may no longer be disturbed.
suggestedAnswer.application: The final ruling of the Court of Appeals, in the same litigation between the same parties, allowed the damages suit to proceed after the registration case. The plaintiff yielded to it in good faith, so the later reversal on the ground of res judicata was wrong.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The reversal was incorrect. **Bar trap:** the presence of all four requisites of res judicata does not end the inquiry; a final, even erroneous, ruling in the same case binds the parties as the law of the case.

keyPoints: Law of the case: what is irrevocably established between the same parties in the same case stays the law of the case, even if wrong
It applies only to that one case and lacks the finality of res judicata
Res judicata binds parties in one case by what was done in another case
The unappealed ruling ordering suspension became final and binding
The plaintiff could not be faulted for pursuing her claim in good faith

source.caseTitle: Padillo v. Court of Appeals, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of res judicata and the law of the case
source.excerpt: However, a different conclusion is warranted under the principle of law of the case. Law of the case has been defined as the opinion delivered on a former appeal. More specifically, it means that whatever is once irrevocably established as the controlling legal rule or decision between the same parties in the same case continues to be the law of the case, whether correct on general principles or not, so long as the facts on which such decision was predicated continue to be the facts of the case before the court. … The appellate court apparently overlooked the significance of this principle called the law of the case which is totally different from the concept of res judicata. Law of the case does not have the finality of the doctrine of res judicata, and applies only to that one case, whereas res judicata forecloses parties or privies in one case by what has been done in another case. … Thus, even if erroneous, the ruling of the Court of Appeals in CA-G.R. SP No. 15356 has become the law of the case as between herein petitioner Padillo and respondent Averia, and may no longer be disturbed or modified.

questions.prompt: A defendant filed a separate suit over the same property while a related case was pending; the suit was dismissed. Under Padillo v. Court of Appeals, does that alone justify moral damages against him?

choices.A: Yes, because every dismissed suit is presumed malicious.
choices.B: Yes, because the plaintiff suffered anxiety from the litigation.
choices.C: Yes, if the plaintiff hired a lawyer.
choices.D: No, because the law could not have meant to impose a penalty on the right to litigate; error alone is not a ground for moral damages.

questions.explanation: **D is correct.** The Court held that filing a suit that was later dismissed "does not per se make such actions or appeals wrongful," since "[t]he law could not have meant to impose a penalty on the right to litigate," and "error alone is not a ground for moral damages." **A is wrong:** malice or bad faith is not presumed. **B is wrong:** the anxiety usually caused to a party hauled into court is not the kind that warrants moral damages. **C is wrong:** hiring a lawyer is irrelevant. **Bar trap:** moral damages for litigation need malice or bad faith.

source.excerpt: That respondent Averia instituted a separate suit which was subsequently dismissed and all actions or appeals taken by respondent Averia relative to M.C. No. 374-82 does not per se make such actions or appeals wrongful and subject respondent Averia to payment of moral damages. The law could not have meant to impose a penalty on the right to litigate. Such right is so precious that moral damages may not be charged on those who may exercise it erroneously. One may have erred, but error alone is not a ground for moral damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: According to Padillo v. Court of Appeals, which of the following is NOT a requisite of res judicata as a bar by prior judgment?

choices.A: The former judgment must be final.
choices.B: Both actions must have been filed in the same court.
choices.C: It must be a judgment or order on the merits.
choices.D: There must be identity of parties, subject matter and cause of action.

questions.explanation: **B is correct**, because it is not a requisite. The four requisites listed are: (1) the former judgment must be final; (2) it must have been rendered by a court having jurisdiction over the subject matter and the parties; (3) it must be a judgment or order on the merits; and (4) identity of parties, subject matter and cause of action. **A, C and D are wrong:** each is a requisite. **Bar trap:** jurisdiction of the first court is required, not that the second case be in the same court.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: X Corp. bought shares of a mining company and asked the company to register the transfer. The company delayed for several months. During the delay, the market price of the shares rose sharply, then fell to below the purchase price. After the transfer was finally made, X Corp. sued for the profit it says it would have made had it been able to sell at the peak. The parties' stipulation of facts says nothing about any plan of X Corp. to sell. Should the claim be granted? Explain, citing Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. Court of Appeals.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The claimed profit is speculative and cannot be recovered.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. CA, the Court held that a claim for unrealized profit must be duly and sufficiently established; the claimant must prove that it was in fact damaged by the defendant's act or omission. Where nothing shows that the claimant intended to sell, or would have sold, the shares on specified dates, whatever profits could have been made are purely speculative, since the rise and fall of share prices cannot be predicted with certainty, and speculative damages cannot be recovered.
suggestedAnswer.application: X Corp. shows only that the price went up and later down. Nothing shows it would have sold at the peak; it could equally have held the shares and waited for further increases. The supposed profit is a guess, not a proved loss.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The claim should be denied. **Bar trap:** a market rise alone does not prove lucro cesante; the claimant must prove that it would actually have earned the profit.

keyPoints: Unrealized profit (lucro cesante) must be duly and sufficiently established
The claimant must prove it was in fact damaged by the defendant's act
No showing that it intended to sell, or would have sold, on specified dates
Share prices rise and fall unpredictably: the profit is purely speculative
Speculative damages cannot be recovered

source.part: Decision, discussion of the first issue (unrealized profits)
source.excerpt: Petitioner company also alleges that the claim for unrealized profit must be duly and sufficiently established, that is, that the claimant must submit proof that it was in fact damaged because of petitioner's act or omission. The stipulation of facts of the parties does not at all show that private respondent intended to sell, or would sell or would have sold the stocks in question on specified dates. While it is true that shares of stock may go up or down in value (as in fact the concerned shares here really rose from fifteen (15) centavos to twenty three or twenty four (23/24) centavos per share and then fell to about two (2) centavos per share, still whatever profits could have been made are purely SPECULATIVE, for it was difficult to predict with any decree of certainty the rise and fall in the value of the shares. Thus this Court has ruled that speculative damages cannot be recovered.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Counsel for a buyer of shares argues: "Had the company transferred the shares when we demanded, we would have sold them and made a profit of ₱5,600. Its refusal deprived us of that profit, so it must pay." How did the Supreme Court answer this argument in Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. Court of Appeals?

suggestedAnswer.answer: The Court rejected it: it is easy to say after the fact that the buyer would have sold and made a profit, but it is equally possible that the buyer's officials would have refused to sell and waited for further increases in value.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Batong Buhay Gold Mines v. CA, the Court said that "human nature, being what it is, private respondent's officials could also have refused to sell and instead wait for expected further increases in value." Because the profit depended on a decision to sell that was never shown, it was speculative, and speculative damages cannot be recovered.
suggestedAnswer.application: The argument assumes the very fact that had to be proved: that the buyer would have sold at the right time. Without proof, the claimed ₱5,600 is hindsight, not a loss caused by the refusal.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The Court set aside the award and reinstated the trial court's decision, which granted no damages. **Bar trap:** hindsight about what a claimant could have done is not proof of what it would have done.

keyPoints: The claimed profit assumes the buyer would have sold at the right time
The buyer's officials could equally have refused to sell and waited
Hindsight is not proof of a loss
The award was set aside and the trial court's decision reinstated

suggestedAnswer.application: The buyer received the shares through the injunction, so the only question was damages for the delay. Because the claimed profit was not proved, nothing was due beyond the transfer itself.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The transfer stood, but no damages were due. **Bar trap:** winning the main relief does not mean an award of damages follows; each item of actual damages must be proved.

questions.prompt: P, a producer, appointed D as its exclusive export distributor for two years, for a commission on every shipment. After seven months, P stopped delivering in breach of the contract, and D sued for the commissions it would have earned for the remaining 17 months. P argues that D cannot recover because it did not prove any actual unfilled sale, any ready buyer or the price such buyers would pay. D proves the volume it shipped and the commissions it earned before the breach. Is D entitled to recover its unearned commissions? Explain, citing General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Yes. Lost profits (lucrum cessans) are recoverable under Article 2200, and D's unearned commissions can be estimated with reasonable certainty from what it earned under the same contract before the breach.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, the Court held that under Article 2200 of the Civil Code, indemnification for damages comprehends not only the value of the loss suffered but also the profits the creditor fails to obtain, so lucrum cessans is a basis for indemnification. The question is whether the creditor failed to make profits because of the breach and whether there is basis for determining such profits with reasonable certainty. Since the distributor had been earning commissions whenever logs were delivered, it was reasonable to expect it would have continued earning in the same manner, and the commission was not difficult to estimate.
suggestedAnswer.application: From D's earnings per unit on past shipments multiplied by the volume P was bound to deliver for the remaining months, the lost commission can be computed. In the case itself, the Court computed ₱365,350.40 and held the ₱400,000 award "not speculative, but based on reasonable estimate."
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: D may recover its unearned commissions. **Bar trap:** compare Batong Buhay v. CA, where a profit depending on an unproved decision to sell was speculative; here the profit rests on a contract and an established earning record.

keyPoints: Art. 2200: damages include the loss suffered and the profits the creditor fails to obtain
Lucrum cessans is a basis for indemnification
Test: profits lost because of the breach, and a basis to determine them with reasonable certainty
Estimate from past commissions per unit times the volume due for the remaining term
The award was a reasonable estimate, not speculative

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the sixth issue (actual damages)
source.excerpt: This argument must be overruled in the light of the law and evidence on the latter. Under Article 2200 of the Civil Code, indemnification for damages comprehends not only the value of the loss suffered but also at of the profits which the creditor fails to obtain. In other words, lucrum cessans is also a basis for indemnification. The question then that arises is: Has appellee failed to make profits because of appellant's breach of contract, and in the affirmative, is there here basis for determining with reasonable certainty such unearned profits? … Had appellant continued to deliver the logs as it was bound to pursuant to the agreement it is reasonable to expect that it would have continued earning its commission in much the same manner as it used to in connection with the previous shipments of logs, which clearly indicates that it failed to earn the commissions it should earn during this period of time. And this commission is not difficult to estimate. … The award therefore, made by the court a quo of the amount of P400,000.00 as compensatory damages is not speculative, but based on reasonable estimate.

questions.prompt: A supply contract allows a party to suspend performance only for listed causes such as fire, flood, strikes, government orders and similar causes beyond its control. The supplier suspends deliveries, citing (a) a demand to renegotiate prices, (b) its plan to build its own processing plant, and (c) new government restrictions and machinery breakdowns. It continued producing and sold its output to other buyers. Was the suspension justified? Explain, citing General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. Grounds (a) and (b) are not among the stipulated causes of suspension, and ground (c), even if fortuitous, did not make it impossible for the supplier to perform.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, the Court held that the demand for renegotiation of prices and the establishment of a veneer plant "are not among the various causes of suspension enumerated" in the contract, so suspension on those grounds was not justified. As to the barter restrictions, breakdowns and the Margin Law, even assuming they were fortuitous, they did not cause such a reduction in production as to make compliance impossible; a fortuitous event does not necessarily extinguish an obligation, as it must be of such a character as to render it impossible for the obligor to fulfill it in a normal manner.
suggestedAnswer.application: The supplier kept producing and sold its output to others, which shows it could have delivered. Its own business plans are not grounds the contract recognizes.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The suspension was a breach, and damages are due. **Bar trap:** labeling an event "fortuitous" is not enough; the obligor must show that the event made normal performance impossible.

keyPoints: Suspension is allowed only for the causes the contract lists
Price renegotiation and a new plant were not listed causes
A fortuitous event must make normal fulfillment impossible to excuse performance
The supplier kept producing and sold to others: no impossibility
The unjustified suspension was a breach

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the second issue (suspension and fortuitous events)
source.excerpt: Even assuming that the restrictions imposed by the government on barter, the breakdown of machineries and the inability to secure spare parts, replacements and wire ropes, as well as the passage of the Margin Law, have the nature of fortuitous events, yet it cannot be said that they had caused such a reduction in appellant's production of logs that made it impossible for it to comply wholly, or even partly, with its commitment with appellee. The rule is that even the happening of a fortuitous event in itself does not necessarily extinguish an obligation for, as this Court has said, the fortuitous event must be of such a character as to render it impossible for the obligor to fulfill his obligation in a normal manner (Lassam v. Smith, 45 Phil. 990). … One of the causes for the suspension of the agreement alleged by appellant was the demand for the renegotiation of prices provided in paragraph 2 of the agreement. Another reason advanced is the establishment of a veneer plant for the purpose of increasing the log production. But these two matters are not among the various causes of suspension enumerated in paragraph 8 of the agreement. The suspension, therefore, of the contract on these causes is not justified.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A party that breached a distribution contract tried to justify its breach with misstatements and half-truths by one of its officers. The trial court awarded the other party ₱100,000 exemplary damages. Should the award be sustained in full? Explain, citing General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging.

suggestedAnswer.answer: Not in full. The award should be reduced, since the breaching party did not act in a wanton, oppressive or malevolent manner; in the case, the Court reduced it to ₱50,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, the Court found the ₱100,000 exemplary damages "somewhat excessive," since the producer, in suspending the contract, "has not acted in a wanton, oppressive or malevolent manner to deserve such a heavy punishment within the purview of the law (Article 2232, new Civil Code)." Its officer's misstatements or half-truths, though reprehensible, were not a wanton or malevolent perversion of the truth, so ₱50,000 was a reasonable exemplary penalty. The attorney's fees were affirmed under Article 2208, considering the importance of the litigation and the time and effort involved.
suggestedAnswer.application: Misstatements meant to justify a breach are blameworthy but fall short of the wanton or malevolent conduct that would warrant a heavy exemplary award in a contract case.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The exemplary damages should be mitigated. **Bar trap:** in contracts, exemplary damages depend on wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive or malevolent conduct (Art. 2232); a reprehensible but not malevolent act justifies only a reduced award.

keyPoints: Exemplary damages in contracts: wanton, oppressive or malevolent conduct (Art. 2232)
Misstatements and half-truths were reprehensible but not wanton or malevolent
₱100,000 was excessive; reduced to ₱50,000
Attorney's fees affirmed under Art. 2208 given the importance of the case and the effort

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the sixth issue (exemplary damages and attorney's fees)
source.excerpt: We believes however, that the amount of P100,000.00 awarded to appellee as exemplary damages is somewhat excessive it appearing that appellant is suspending the operation of the contract has not acted in a wanton, oppressive or malevolent manner to deserve such a heavy punishment within the purview of the law (Article 2232, new Civil Code). The most that can be said is that appellant, to suit its purpose, has availed to certain misstatements or half truths as reflected in the declarations of Mr. Dempsey, one of its high officials, in an attempt to justify its desistance from the contract. While this is reprehensible, it is not a wanton or malevolent perversion of the truth. Hence, the award should be mitigated and in our opinion the amount of P50,000.00 is a reasonable exemplary penalty. We also find reasonable the amount awarded by the court a quo as attorney's fees considering the importance of this litigation and the amount of time and effort therein involved. This is justified under Article 2208 of the Civil Code.

questions.prompt: Under Article 2200 of the Civil Code, as applied in General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, indemnification for damages comprehends

choices.A: only the value of the loss suffered.
choices.B: only the profits the creditor fails to obtain.
choices.C: not only the value of the loss suffered but also the profits which the creditor fails to obtain.
choices.D: only damages that were foreseen at the time the contract was made, excluding profits.

questions.explanation: **C is correct.** The Court said: "Under Article 2200 of the Civil Code, indemnification for damages comprehends not only the value of the loss suffered but also at of the profits which the creditor fails to obtain. In other words, lucrum cessans is also a basis for indemnification." **A and B are wrong:** each states only half the rule. **D is wrong:** Article 2200 expressly covers unrealized profits. **Bar trap:** the two components are daño emergente (loss suffered) and lucro cesante (profits lost).

questions.prompt: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, how did the Court determine the distributor's lost commissions?

choices.A: By the distributor's own estimate of its expected profits.
choices.B: By multiplying the volume the producer was bound to deliver in the remaining 17 months by the commission per board foot the distributor actually earned on earlier shipments.
choices.C: By awarding nominal damages, since lost profits are inherently speculative.
choices.D: By the market value of the logs the producer sold to other buyers.

source.caseTitle: General Enterprises, Inc. v. Lianga Bay Logging Co., Inc.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the sixth issue (actual damages)
source.excerpt: Thus, during the seventeen remaining months of the contract, at the rate of at least 2,000,000 board feet, appellant should have delivered thirty-four million board feet. Multiplying 34 million board feet by P.0107456, the product is P365,350.40, which represents the lucrum cessans that should accrue to appellee.

questions.prompt: In General Enterprises v. Lianga Bay Logging, the Court defined the cause of a contract as

choices.A: the essential reason which moves the contracting parties to enter into it.
choices.B: the motive of each party, whatever it may be.
choices.C: the object of the contract.
choices.D: the consent of the parties.

For the producer, it was the distribution of its logs; for the distributor, the sale of the logs for a commission. **B is wrong:** motives are distinct from cause. **C and D are wrong:** object and consent are different requisites. **Bar trap:** a side promise not in the contract was not its cause.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A bus crashed into the terrace of O's building. To prove her actual damages, O presented (a) a written cost estimate of ₱171,000 prepared by an engineer who never testified, (b) a receipt of ₱35,000 for repair work, and (c) her own testimony that the damage was severe. The bus owner's architect testified that repairs would cost ₱55,000. The trial court awarded ₱150,000 without explaining how it arrived at that figure. Is the award correct? What amount should be awarded? Explain, citing Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The ₱150,000 award has no factual basis. Actual damages must be proved with a reasonable degree of certainty, and the evidence supports only ₱55,000.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Marikina Auto Line v. People, the Court held that actual damages are not presumed: the claimant must prove the actual amount of loss with a reasonable degree of certainty premised upon competent proof and on the best evidence obtainable, pointing out specific facts that afford a basis for measuring them; they cannot rest on surmises or conjectures. A claimant's bare testimonial assertions should be admitted with extreme caution and buttressed by independent evidence, and an estimate of the damage cost will not suffice.
suggestedAnswer.application: The engineer's estimate is unsupported since he did not testify; O's own testimony is self-interested. Neither the trial court nor the Court of Appeals stated the basis of its award. In the case, the Court awarded ₱55,000, the amount shown by the defendants' own evidence.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The award should be reduced to ₱55,000. **Bar trap:** a repair estimate or a court's unexplained figure is not proof of actual loss; look for competent evidence of the actual amount.

keyPoints: Actual damages are not presumed
Prove the actual loss with reasonable certainty, on competent proof and the best evidence obtainable
Point out specific facts that afford a basis for measuring the damages
Bare self-serving testimony: admit with extreme caution; an estimate will not suffice
Award based on the defense's own evidence: ₱55,000

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the second issue (actual damages)
source.excerpt: The burden of proof is on the party who would be defeated if no evidence would be presented on either side. The burden is to establish one’s case by a preponderance of evidence which means that the evidence, as a whole, adduced by one side, is superior to that of the other. Actual damages are not presumed. The claimant must prove the actual amount of loss with a reasonable degree of certainty premised upon competent proof and on the best evidence obtainable. Specific facts that could afford a basis for measuring whatever compensatory or actual damages are borne must be pointed out. Actual damages cannot be anchored on mere surmises, speculations or conjectures. … While claimants’ bare testimonial assertions in support of their claims for damages should not be discarded altogether, however, the same should be admitted with extreme caution. Their testimonies should be viewed in light of claimants’ self-interest, hence, should not be taken as gospel truth. Such assertion should be buttressed by independent evidence. … An estimate of the damage cost will not suffice: … We note, however, that petitioners adduced evidence that, in their view, the cost of the damage to the terrace of private respondent would amount to P55,000.00. Accordingly, private respondent is entitled to P55,000.00 actual damages.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: Charged with reckless imprudence resulting in damage to property, a bus driver who swerved into a building invokes the sudden emergency rule, claiming he had to avoid a jeepney that intruded into his lane. In his counter-affidavit, however, he said he swerved because the jeepney ahead suddenly stopped. Photographs show heavy damage to the building. Will the defense prosper? Explain, citing Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. The sudden emergency rule was not proved, and the evidence shows the driver's own negligence.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Marikina Auto Line v. People, the Court quoted the sudden emergency rule: one who suddenly finds himself in a place of danger and must act without time to consider the best means to avoid it is not guilty of negligence if he fails to adopt what later appears a better method, "unless the emergency in which he finds himself is brought about by his own negligence." The burden was on the driver to prove that he acted in an emergency. Under Article 2185, a person driving a motor vehicle is presumed negligent if at the time of the mishap he was violating a traffic regulation; by his own admission, the driver violated the Land Transportation and Traffic Code when he suddenly swerved to the right.
suggestedAnswer.application: The heavy damage showed a strong impact and a speeding bus; had he not been speeding, he could have stopped. His conflicting statements destroyed his credibility. And if the jeepney were really to blame, he could have filed a third-party complaint against its driver and owner.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The defense fails, and the driver is liable. **Bar trap:** the sudden emergency rule does not protect one whose own negligence (here, speeding) created the emergency, and the one invoking it must prove it.

keyPoints: Sudden emergency rule: no negligence for failing to choose the best means in a sudden danger
Not if the emergency was brought about by one's own negligence
The one invoking it bears the burden of proof
Presumption of negligence when violating a traffic regulation (Art. 2185)
Heavy damage showed speeding; inconsistent statements destroyed credibility

source.caseTitle: Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation, et al. v. People, et al.
source.part: Decision, discussion of the first issue (sudden emergency rule)
source.excerpt: It was the burden of petitioners herein to prove petitioner Suelto’s defense that he acted on an emergency, that is, he had to swerve the bus to the right to avoid colliding with a passenger jeep coming from EDSA that had overtaken another vehicle and intruded into the lane of the bus. The sudden emergency rule was enunciated by this Court in Gan v. Court of Appeals, thus: [O]ne who suddenly finds himself in a place of danger, and is required to act without time to consider the best means that may be adopted to avoid the impending danger, is not guilty of negligence if he fails to adopt what subsequently and upon reflection may appear to have been a better method unless the emergency in which he finds himself is brought about by his own negligence. … In relation thereto, Article 2185 of the New Civil Code provides that "unless there is proof to the contrary, it is presumed that a person driving a motor vehicle has been negligent, if at the time of mishap, he was violating any traffic regulation." By his own admission, petitioner Suelto violated the Land Transportation and Traffic Code when he suddenly swerved the bus to the right, thereby causing damage to the property of private respondent.

questions.subject: Civil Law
questions.prompt: A driver is convicted of reckless imprudence that resulted only in damage to another's property worth ₱55,000. The trial court sentenced him to a straight term of one year of imprisonment. Is the penalty correct? Explain, citing Marikina Auto Line Transport Corporation v. People.

suggestedAnswer.answer: No. When reckless imprudence results only in damage to property, the penalty under Article 365 of the Revised Penal Code is a fine, not imprisonment.
suggestedAnswer.legalBasis: In Marikina Auto Line v. People, the Court held that under the third paragraph of Article 365, "[w]hen the execution of the act covered by this article shall have only resulted in damage to the property of another, the offender shall be punished by a fine ranging from an amount equal to the value of said damages to three times such value, but which shall in no case be less than 25 pesos."
suggestedAnswer.application: Since the only damage was to the terrace, worth ₱55,000, the driver should be fined. In the case, the Court sentenced him to a fine of ₱55,000 with subsidiary imprisonment in case of insolvency.
suggestedAnswer.conclusion: The prison term should be replaced by a fine. **Bar trap:** the penalty for imprudence resulting only in damage to property is a fine measured by the value of the damage, from once to three times that value.

keyPoints: Art. 365, third paragraph: damage to property only = a fine
Fine from the value of the damage to three times that value, not less than ₱25
A straight prison term was erroneous
Fine of ₱55,000 with subsidiary imprisonment in case of insolvency
